title: Is Organic Food Really Worth It?
summary: Explainer on USDA organic labelling categories, price premiums, mixed evidence on safety and nutrition, and weak fraud enforcement for imported grain.

assertions.quote: product needs to have more than 95% in order to carry that USDA seal
Multi-ingredient products with less than 70% certified organic content cannot use the organic seal

verdicts.note: 7 CFR 205.301(c) requires 'made with organic (specified ingredients)' products to contain at least 70 percent organic ingredients, excluding water and salt.
"Made with organic" products must contain at least 70 percent organic ingredients, must be certified, and may not carry the seal.

assertions.quote: fed 100% organic feed and not administered antibiotics or hormones
Organic does not mean that the produce is grown without any pesticides.
the pesticide residue in both organic and conventional crops are too low to have any adverse effects on health
concluded that there was no significant difference in nutrition between organic and conventional crops
But rarely does it mean actually testing the soil or produce

verdicts.note: USDA requires certifiers to residue-test only about 5 percent of operations a year; certification otherwise rests on records and inspections.

The required floor is low: under 7 CFR 205.670(d) certifiers need sample only 5 percent of operations a year, plus for-cause tests, so most operations need not be tested in a given year; the rule says nothing about how much testing certifiers do above that floor.

assertions.quote: imported produce is more likely to be fraudulent than domestic grown crops

verdicts.note: OIG (2017) found AMS could not reasonably assure that import certificates were checked at ports and had no controls to keep fumigated imports from being sold as organic, which raises the risk for imports; it measured no fraud rate, and the findings predate the SOE rule.

assertions.quote: The organic fraud in grains started cause of the high demand for especially eggs and meat

verdicts.note: Prosecuted cases involved millions of bushels of conventional corn and soy sold as organic livestock feed.
